q: Which properties make ATP suitable as an immediately available energy source rather than a long-term energy store?
options: It releases a small, usable packet of energy in one step and is soluble, so it moves quickly around the cell
It holds more energy per molecule than glucose and is insoluble, so it can be packed densely in cells for later use
It is very stable, so it can accumulate in large quantities and be released gradually over many hours
It can only be hydrolysed inside mitochondria, which keeps its energy safely locked away until needed
explanation: Hydrolysis of ATP releases a modest packet of energy (~30.5 kJ/mol) in a single step – enough for typical cellular tasks without wasting much as heat. ATP is water-soluble, diffuses rapidly through the cytoplasm and is hydrolysed wherever energy is needed. But it is relatively unstable and present only in small amounts, so long-term stores are glycogen, starch and lipids.
